title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how K-12 mathematics educators evaluate and prefer generative-AI-produced lesson plans compared with human-created lesson plans. The core question is whether lesson plans generated by a customized GPT-4 model and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model can match or exceed the pedagogical quality of plans authored by human curriculum designers, and how those preferences vary by lesson component and grade level. The study is motivated by growing teacher use of GenAI for lesson planning alongside concerns that general-purpose AI may produce pedagogically weak, inaccurate, or insufficiently differentiated materials.

The researchers conducted a comparative preference study using 400 mathematics lesson-plan queries aligned to Common Core standards. For each query, three lesson plans were available: one from a customized GPT-4 system, one from a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model, and one human-authored plan retrieved from open educational repositories. Experienced K-12 math educators completed blinded pairwise comparisons of lesson plans on warm-up quality, main task quality, cool-down quality, and overall preference, and also provided open-ended comments. The analysis combined quantitative pairwise preference comparisons and bootstrapping with qualitative thematic analysis and LDA topic modeling of educator comments.

The study involved experienced K-12 mathematics educators in the United States, with evaluations spanning elementary, middle, and high school lesson plans. Sixteen educators contributed data to the final analysis after four participants withdrew. Data collection occurred over several weeks from March to July 2024 via a web-based platform, with participants evaluating lesson-plan pairs assigned to their grade-level expertise.

The main conclusion is that human-authored lesson plans remained generally preferred overall, especially in elementary grades and for warm-up and main instructional tasks, where educators valued scaffolding, student discourse, differentiation, and developmental appropriateness. However, AI-generated lesson plans were competitive in some areas, especially cool-down sections, and became more competitive in middle and high school contexts. GPT-4 was especially strong for structured lesson conclusions, while fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b showed stronger performance in high-school content complexity. The authors conclude that GenAI is best understood as a collaborative assistive tool for lesson planning rather than a replacement for educator expertise.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used to generate text content; in this paper, a customized prompt-based GPT-4 model generated lesson plans.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate K-12 mathematics lesson plans from prompts containing subject, grade level, CCSSM standard, lesson title, and learning objectives; educator preferences were compared against human-created plans and a fine-tuned LLaMA model.

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise comparisons across all measures, the customized GPT-4 model was preferred over the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model 57.7% to 42.3%, but was less preferred than human curriculum designer lesson plans 41.3% to 58.7%. The study used 529 unique evaluated lesson plan pairs from 16 educators, yielding 2,116 total evaluations.
findings.measure: Educator pairwise preference ratings across warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality for lesson plans

findings.finding_summary: By lesson plan component, the customized GPT-4 model underperformed human-authored plans on warm-up (35.9% vs 64.1%), main tasks (33.0% vs 67.0%), and overall quality (36.4% vs 63.6%), but outperformed human-authored plans on cool-down activities (59.7% vs 40.3%). The authors interpret GPT-4 as especially effective for structured lesson wrap-ups and summarization tasks.
findings.measure: Educator pairwise preference by lesson plan section
findings.effect_size: Warm-up 35.9% vs 64.1%; Main tasks 33.0% vs 67.0%; Cool-down 59.7% vs 40.3%; Overall 36.4% vs 63.6%

findings.finding_summary: Preferences for the customized GPT-4 model varied by grade level. In elementary school, human-authored plans were preferred over GPT-4 61.5% to 38.5%; in middle school, GPT-4 was preferred over human-authored plans 54.5% to 45.5%; and against fine-tuned LLaMA, GPT-4 was preferred 60.7% in elementary, 56.9% in middle school, and 54.6% in high school. These results indicate stronger competitiveness of GPT-4 in middle and upper grades than in elementary contexts.
findings.measure: Educator pairwise preference by grade level
findings.effect_size: Vs human: elementary 38.5% vs 61.5%; middle 54.5% vs 45.5%; Vs LLaMA: elementary 60.7% vs 39.3%; middle 56.9% vs 43.1%; high school 54.6% vs 45.4%

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta LLaMA-family large language model; in this paper, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model trained on expert-designed lesson plans generated lesson plans.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate K-12 mathematics lesson plans after fine-tuning on expert-designed lesson plans; educator preferences were compared against human-created plans and a customized GPT-4 model.

findings.finding_summary: Across all measures, the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model was preferred less often than the customized GPT-4 model (42.3% vs 57.7%) and slightly less often than human curriculum designer plans (46.4% vs 53.6%). The smaller gap versus human-authored plans than GPT-4's gap suggests competitive performance overall.
findings.measure: Educator pairwise preference ratings across warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality for lesson plans

findings.finding_summary: By lesson plan component, the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model was less preferred than human-authored plans on warm-up (43.2% vs 56.8%), main tasks (40.5% vs 59.5%), and overall quality (44.2% vs 55.8%), but outperformed human-authored plans on cool-down activities (57.9% vs 42.1%). The paper highlights this as evidence that AI-generated conclusions and structured summaries were well received.
findings.measure: Educator pairwise preference by lesson plan section
findings.effect_size: Warm-up 43.2% vs 56.8%; Main tasks 40.5% vs 59.5%; Cool-down 57.9% vs 42.1%; Overall 44.2% vs 55.8%

findings.finding_summary: Grade-level results favored human-authored plans in elementary school, where LLaMA was preferred 35.1% versus 64.9% for human plans, but shifted in upper grades. In middle school, LLaMA was narrowly preferred over human-authored plans 50.7% to 49.3%, and in high school LLaMA was preferred 59.2% to 40.8% over human-authored plans. The authors interpret this as a transition toward stronger AI competitiveness at higher grade levels.
findings.measure: Educator pairwise preference by grade level
findings.effect_size: Vs human: elementary 35.1% vs 64.9%; middle 50.7% vs 49.3%; high school 59.2% vs 40.8%

quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-methods preference study with blinded pairwise evaluations by experienced educators, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experimental study measuring student outcomes. Outcomes are based on educator judgments of lesson plan quality and usability rather than causal effects on learning.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports preference shares rather than standardized effect sizes or student achievement impacts, so impact magnitude is unclear. Results are practically suggestive for lesson-planning assistance, especially for cool-down tasks and upper-grade content, but do not establish clear educational impact on learners.
